==Problem==
The faces of each of two fair dice are numbered <imath>1</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, <imath>5</imath>, <imath>7</imath>, and <imath>8</imath>. When the two dice are tossed, what is the probability that their sum will be an even number?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }\frac{4}{9}\qquad\textbf{(B) }\frac{1}{2}\qquad\textbf{(C) }\frac{5}{9}\qquad\textbf{(D) }\frac{3}{5}\qquad\textbf{(E) }\frac{2}{3}</imath>

==Solution 1 (Casework)==
We have <imath>2</imath> dice with <imath>2</imath> evens and <imath>4</imath> odds on each die. For the sum to be even, the 2 rolls must be <imath>2</imath> odds or <imath>2</imath> evens. 

Ways to roll <imath>2</imath> odds (Case <imath>1</imath>): The total number of ways to obtain <imath>2</imath> odds on 2 rolls is <imath>4*4=16</imath>, as there are <imath>4</imath> possible odds on the first roll and <imath>4</imath> possible odds on the second roll.

Ways to roll <imath>2</imath> evens (Case <imath>2</imath>): Similarly, we have <imath>2*2=4</imath> ways to obtain 2 evens. Probability is <imath>\frac{20}{36}=\frac{5}{9}</imath>, or <imath>\framebox{C}</imath>.

==Solution 2 (Complementary Counting)==
We count the ways to get an odd. If the sum is odd, then we must have an even and an odd. The probability of an even is <imath>\frac{1}{3}</imath> , and the probability of an odd is <imath>\frac{2}{3}</imath>. We have to multiply by <imath>2</imath> because the even and odd can be in any order. This gets us <imath>\frac{4}{9}</imath>, so the answer is <imath>1 - \frac{4}{9} = \frac{5}{9} = \boxed{(\textbf{C})}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
To get an even, you must get either 2 odds or 2 evens. The probability of getting 2 odds is <imath>\frac{4}{6} \times \frac{4}{6}</imath>. The probability of getting 2 evens is <imath>\frac{2}{6} \times \frac{2}{6}</imath>. If you add them together, you get <imath>\frac{16}{36} + \frac{4}{36}</imath> = <imath>\boxed{(\textbf{C})  \frac{5}{9}}</imath>.
